results.summary: This design implements a 4-bit 2-stage FIR filter that multiplies input samples by tap coefficients and sums the results. Coefficients are loaded serially by setting values and pulsing the load signal twice per tap, and the filter runs by changing the input each clock cycle. Select pins allow debugging by routing internal signals such as multiplier outputs or stored tap values to the output pins. The FIR output discards the least significant bit due to output pin limitations, and external hardware such as an Arduino or FPGA is needed to drive inputs and read results.

This project generates a rotating dash animation on a six-segment display, driven by an external clock. It can run continuously or be stepped manually using a mode switch and a step button, with a low-active reset. The design is intended for the default PCB and uses DIP switches for control. Documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation.

This is a phase/frequency detector block intended for use in a phase-locked loop, comparing a reference clock and a feedback clock. It outputs up and inverted down signals that indicate the phase difference, with the up signal active when the feedback leads and down when it lags. The design requires external signal generators for square wave inputs to test. It is a building block for PLL systems and is implemented in Wokwi.

This design produces siren-like tones and light patterns reminiscent of 1970s effects, using a chain of D flip-flops to divide the clock into various frequencies. Higher frequencies generate tones for audio output, while lower frequencies control the patterns on a seven-segment display and modulate the tones. A pattern select input chooses between two groups of patterns. External hardware such as a speaker with a series resistor or an audio amplifier is required for sound output.

This project is a tiny synthesizer that generates a C scale by modulating the clock frequency based on input pins corresponding to notes C through B. It outputs square waves at four octave-related pitches. The documentation is incomplete, with the author noting they will add more details later, and the external hardware needed to make sound is not fully determined. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires a clock input.

This design generates and checks PRBS15 sequences using an LFSR. It can be enabled to generate the sequence and, when in check mode, compares the output to detect errors. Testing requires a logic analyzer and jumper leads to monitor the error and checked signals. The design is a straightforward implementation of a pseudo-random bit sequence generator and checker.

This project displays an animation of a segmented worm traveling along a pseudo-random path on a seven-segment LED display. It includes controls for disabling auto-reset, manual reset, and a turbo mode that bypasses a clock divider. The number of worm segments can be set to two or three. The design is a simple animation demo and requires only the default PCB for use.

This design is a test circuit for various flip-flop types, including D, C, S, R, NAND-based, and Muller configurations. Inputs are provided to select and control the flip-flops, and outputs drive a seven-segment display to show their states. The documentation states it is 'nothing special - just testing' and suggests changing inputs to observe outputs. A logic analyzer is listed as external hardware for debugging.

This design computes the dot product of two 2-element vectors, each element being a 2-bit integer. The inputs are packed into the 8 input pins, and the result is displayed on a seven-segment display. The documentation provides a test example: setting input to 11011010 yields an output of 00001000. The design is a simple arithmetic unit implemented in Wokwi.

This design implements a single cell of Conway's Game of Life, calculating whether the cell survives or dies based on the number of neighbours and its current state. It uses five inputs to represent up to nine neighbours in two stages, with a half-select signal to switch between stages. The output is shown on a seven-segment display, and an inverted clock is provided. External hardware is needed to supply the neighbour states and reroute the current state.
